title: Delhi locks down for CJP's October 10 protest amid court plea, gurdwara refuge, trader backlash
excerpt: New Delhi heads into a near-total lockdown Friday night ahead of the Citizens for Justice and Peace protest at Jantar Mantar — with 57 metro stations shut, trains cancelled, internet curbed in central Delhi, a Supreme Court plea against the curbs, protesters sheltered at Bangla Sahib Gurdwara, and traders demanding a protest ban through Diwali.
body:
• What this means for you: Entry and exit gates at 57 Delhi metro stations close from 9 pm on Friday, October 9 through Saturday, October 10; more than 60 trains arriving at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm Saturday are cancelled; and mobile internet goes dark from 10 pm Friday to 10 pm Saturday in parts of central Delhi including Connaught Place, Khan Market and Jangpura.
  • The Supreme Court heard an urgent plea challenging the sweep of the curbs — a contempt plea was filed over the DMRC station closures — and told authorities they cannot bring everything to a halt; metro and trains must run in a suitably regulated manner.
  • CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said the October 10 march must continue even if he is arrested, while actor Prakash Raj attacked the cancelled trains and preventive detentions ahead of the protest.
  • Delhi's traders' body, the Chamber of Trade and Industry, has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding a ban on large protests in central Delhi from Navratri to Diwali, claiming business activity has dropped 70% in three days — a figure that has not been independently verified.

New Delhi entered a near-total lockdown on Friday evening ahead of the Citizens for Justice and Peace (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, October 10. Delhi Police shut the entry and exit gates of 57 metro stations, ordered a 24-hour mobile internet shutdown in parts of central Delhi, cancelled dozens of trains into the capital and set up 37 blocking points across the New Delhi district — measures whose scale the Supreme Court questioned in an urgent hearing the same day.

The restrictions were imposed after police denied permission for the demonstration. Joint Commissioner of Police Nupur Prasad said the application was submitted on October 7, just three days before the proposed gathering, against a prescribed notice period of at least 10 days. Police also cited alleged violations of undertakings given during an earlier protest at the same site. The security posture builds on the deployment we reported on October 8, when the capital began moving toward a 26,000-strong central force presence.

Context & Background

The protest has been called by the Citizens for Justice and Peace — styled as the Cockroach Janta Party and founded by Abhijeet Dipke — along with student groups such as the All India Students' Association (AISA). The demands are the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the electoral rolls, the scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, and an independent, neutral procedure for selecting Election Commissioners. Dipke said CJP is fighting for free and fair elections and that the commissioner-selection process must be neutral and independent.

https://x.com/WIONews/status/2108552087395291600

Friday's developments pushed the standoff into new territory. A plea — reported as a contempt plea — was filed in the Supreme Court challenging the closure of the DMRC station gates. In court, senior advocate Kapil Sibal flagged the train cancellations, the 57 metro station closures, internet curbs and hotel booking bans; A.M. Singhvi described the measures as unprecedented in scale, citing the deployment of hundreds of central force companies, preparations for detention centres and restrictions affecting transport and hotel bookings; and advocate Vrinda Grover said extensive barricading could make access to Jantar Mantar difficult despite its status as a designated protest venue. Justice Bagchi's bench observed that a gathering without the requisite authorisation would be unlawful, but said restrictions must satisfy the test of proportionality.

Impact & Analysis

The curbs are the broadest imposed on the capital in recent memory. DMRC said entry and exit gates at the 57 stations would stay closed from 9 pm on October 9 through October 10, covering Rajiv Chowk, Central Secretariat, Kashmere Gate, Mandi House, New Delhi and other hubs; interchange remains available except at the New Delhi station. The Supreme Court declined to order a full shutdown, directing the Centre and authorities to ensure public transport keeps running in a regulated manner rather than being brought to a complete halt.

Communications are affected too: the Deputy Commissioner of Police ordered mobile internet services suspended from 10 pm Friday to 10 pm Saturday across zones including Connaught Place, Mandi House, Pragati Maidan, the Gurdwara Bangla Sahib area, Barakhamba Road, Khan Market, Lodhi Road and Jangpura, communicated to operators including Airtel, Jio, Vodafone Idea and MTNL. Rail passengers face the cancellation of more than 60 trains arriving at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm on Saturday. Police say passengers with valid tickets will not be stopped from travelling.

As the curbs tightened, India Today footage showed protesters taking shelter at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib ahead of the protest. The response drew a sharp reaction from actor Prakash Raj, a supporter of the campaign, who posted a video on X questioning why citizens were being stopped from travelling and assembling.

"Cancelling trains, picking up people from their homes, arresting them on their way to the protest site... Cheating karta hai tu, cheating! Nahi chalega. Just asking."

— Prakash Raj, actor

Two groups linked to the All India Students' Federation alleged railway police tried to stop them at Bhusawal and Itarsi stations en route to Delhi, and CJP has alleged supporters travelling to the capital are being detained in several states. Police have meanwhile set up dedicated detention centres in each district and are checking hotels, guest houses and bus terminals.

The commercial fallout prompted the Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) to write to Prime Minister Modi demanding that large protests be barred from central Delhi — including Jantar Mantar, Parliament Street and Lutyens' Delhi — from Navratri until Diwali. CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal said a traders' survey showed business activity down 70% over three days and daily outstation shoppers falling from 2-3 lakh to 40,000-50,000, figures that have not been independently verified. The body also proposed a permanent protest zone at Burari or Ramlila Maidan. Traders' associations warned the festive season could face disruptions worth ₹250 crore daily, and backed keeping Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar and Connaught Place accessible.

"Politics has its own place, and business has its own."

— Joint statement, Delhi trade associations

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs and visitors currently in Delhi — festival season is a peak window for homecoming travel — the immediate concern is practical: check DMRC service updates and train status before stepping out on Friday night or Saturday, and expect spotty mobile data in central Delhi. Beyond logistics, the standoff touches a question the diaspora follows closely: the credibility of India's electoral rolls and the machinery of the vote. The SIR exercise and the commissioner-appointment process Dipke is challenging are the same institutional plumbing that determines whether votes — including those of a diaspora that travels home to cast them — are counted fairly.

What's Next

The immediate test is Saturday itself. In a video message released late Friday night, Dipke appealed to supporters to gather in large numbers at Jantar Mantar and said the march should continue peacefully even if he is arrested or detained. The Supreme Court, meanwhile, has asked authorities to reconsider the restrictions and keep public transport running in regulated form, with the possibility of urgent consideration by the Delhi High Court also discussed. How much of the lockdown is rolled back — and whether the protest proceeds at the venue despite the denied permission — will determine whether the standoff de-escalates or deepens. And with traders now demanding a ban on large protests in central Delhi through the Diwali season, the question of where Delhi allows dissent is becoming a fight in its own right.
